lead.headline: OpenAI lets agents check out with a Wallet as United blocks outside AI agents
lead.dek: Agent shopping launches to a limited group of US Pro subscribers the same week an airline moves to shut third-party assistants out of its booking systems.

bottom_line: OpenAI launched a Wallet that lets its agents complete purchases for a limited group of US Pro subscribers, while United Airlines said it will restrict outside AI agents from booking flights. Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen as its new fast tier, and a researcher's analysis of model weights claims leading Chinese open models were trained on banned Blackwell chips. Anthropic published guidance on building safety evaluations.

front.summary: Agent commerce dominates the day: OpenAI launched a Wallet for its agents and Meta's Muse gained phone calling, while United moved to block outside agents. Google's Hydrogen release rests mostly on Google's own benchmark claims. TSMC's planned stakes and a chip-fingerprint analysis tie the labs to the hardware supply chain.

axes.name: Google DeepMind
axes.text: Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen as its new fast tier, replacing Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google says it is 2.5 times faster and cuts fabricated claims more than fivefold; Latent Space adds Artificial Analysis results that are strong on hallucination but weaker on terminal tasks.

axes.name: OpenAI
axes.text: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents, called dots, complete purchases with a payment token. It starts with a limited number of US Pro subscribers, who approve each purchase with a security check.

axes.name: Meta
axes.text: Meta's Muse agent can now place phone calls to US businesses for paid subscribers, announced by Alexandr Wang. TechCrunch says Muse has over 10 million users, per the company, and plans start at $20 a month.

axes.name: Anthropic
axes.text: Anthropic published a guide to building strong safety evaluations, drawing on its system cards. Separately, TSMC's board reportedly approved $500 million of Anthropic stock at the expected IPO price.

axes.name: NaiveAI
axes.text: The Chinese company's open-weights Naive-N0.5-Flash promises about 2,100 tokens per second. Latent Space's hands-on test found its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek, at a slightly higher cost per question.

axes.name: TSMC
axes.text: TSMC's board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock and $500 million in Anthropic shares, according to Reuters as cited by Ars Technica. The Wall Street Journal notes analysts worry about circular financing.

axes.name: LangChain
axes.text: The agent-management startup raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG. It says it has 7,000 LangSmith customers.

axes.name: Chinese open models
axes.text: Researcher Will DePue says weights of models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry fingerprints of Blackwell training. TechCrunch notes the chips could have been used in an offshore data center, so a rule may not have been broken.

sections.summary: Google's Hydrogen was the day's main release, with most performance figures coming from Google. An older hands-on test covers a fast open-weights coding model.

items.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen to replace Gemini 3.8 Flash
items.summary: Google says Hydrogen is 2.5 times faster than the model it replaces and cuts fabricated claims more than fivefold. API pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output, per Ars Technica. Latent Space adds independent Artificial Analysis results that are strong on hallucination but weaker on terminal tasks.

items.headline: From November 10: Latent Space tests NaiveAI's fast open coding model
items.summary: NaiveAI's Naive-N0.5-Flash is an open-weights model tuned for speed, promising about 2,100 tokens per second. Latent Space's reviewer found its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek and GLM, at a slightly higher cost per question.

sections.summary: Findings range from a verification milestone to a contested claim about chips behind Chinese models. Each comes with limits stated by its authors or reporters.

items.headline: Researcher says Chinese open models bear Blackwell fingerprints
items.summary: Will DePue of Unemployment Labs analysed weights from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group and says they show Blackwell training. TechCrunch notes the chips could have run in an offshore data center, so export rules may not have been broken.

items.headline: Anthropic sets out how to build strong safety evaluations
items.summary: The post recommends matching the design to the question, measuring appropriate responses rather than refusals, and testing multi-turn conversations. It draws on examples from Anthropic's own system cards.

items.headline: From November 11: DeepMind formally verifies parts of the Signal protocol
items.summary: Researchers used an agentic framework called AlphaProof Code to verify key guarantees in four weeks and found no new flaws in the covered parts. They say the work is limited in scope and much remains before it scales.

items.headline: OpenAI board member Cristiano describes takeover risk in a lecture
items.summary: Paul Cristiano, who sits on the OpenAI Foundation board, said an AI accident is the likeliest cause of death for most of the audience. He admitted no quantitative model supports a probability, so the figures are his own estimate.

sections.summary: Agents moved toward payments and phone calls, and one major company moved to keep outside agents out. A coding agent's sharing links added a security lesson.

items.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for agent purchases
items.summary: OpenAI's agents, called dots, can complete purchases using a payment token rather than raw card details. It starts with a limited number of US Pro subscribers, who approve each purchase with a security check.

items.headline: United Airlines moves to block third-party AI agents from booking
items.summary: United said sharing credentials with outside AI assistants can lead to unintended purchases and may conflict with federal check-in rules. It will restrict access directly and through travel agencies and aggregators.

items.headline: Meta's Muse agent can now call US businesses for paying users
items.summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, announced the feature for paid US subscribers. Muse plans start at $20 a month, and Meta says the agent has over 10 million users.

items.headline: From November 10: Claroc reports Grok Build sharing links expose user data
items.summary: Claroc says shared Grok Build apps could be enumerated, exposing business and personal data, including from 24 SpaceXSI apps. SpaceXSI began removing the links after Ars Technica sent questions.

sections.summary: Money flowed toward the labs and their tooling: TSMC planned stakes in two labs and LangChain doubled its valuation. Analysts quoted by the Wall Street Journal cautioned about circular financing.

items.headline: From November 11: TSMC plans up to $1 billion in OpenAI and Anthropic
items.summary: Reuters reports the board approved up to $500 million of OpenAI preferred stock and $500 million of Anthropic shares at the expected IPO price. The Wall Street Journal quotes analysts warning that circular financing obscures real demand.

items.headline: LangChain raises $300 million at a $3 billion valuation
items.summary: CapitalG led the Series C, more than double the company's valuation a year ago. LangChain says it has 7,000 LangSmith customers, including Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce.

explainer.title: What a system one model is, and how it differs from a chatbot
explainer.text:
A system one model does not write paragraphs. It returns a structured choice, a score or a probability, for example which category a request belongs to. Latent Space describes these as non-generative models that are typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning language models, which it calls system two models.

At this week's AI Engineer Code Summit, speakers argued these models belong inside application code, where a program needs a reliable decision rather than a long answer. Diogo Almeida of TypeSafe AI said language models can be brilliant most of the time and poor the rest, which is hard to automate around.

Chinmay Goyal of Glean said the company uses such models next to language models and does not need to fine-tune them again when its categories change.

playbook.title: Score whole conversations against an expert rubric, not single refusals
playbook.who: Anthropic, in its post on building strong safety evaluations
playbook.summary: A refusal rate can reward a model that simply declines everything. Anthropic recommends judging whether the model behaved appropriately across a whole simulated conversation, using a rubric written by domain experts. Use it when you test any assistant for risky topics.
steps: Have a domain expert write a rubric for the risk area that defines an appropriate response.
Pair harmful prompts with benign ones on the same topic to catch over-refusal.
Fix the first user turn and let a model play the user for later turns.
Fail the whole conversation if any single turn goes wrong.
Run the evals in a sandbox with no internet and monitor them live.

playbook.title: Call a fast classifier model inside your code when you need a decision
playbook.who: Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, and Chinmay Goyal of Glean
playbook.summary: Reasoning models are slow and sometimes unreliable for simple decisions. System one models return a choice, score or probability quickly and cheaply, so they can sit inside ordinary code. Use them for routing, labelling and extraction, and keep language models for open-ended writing.
steps: Pick a decision in your app that currently relies on a long prompt, such as routing or labelling.
Replace it with a call to a system one model that returns a structured choice or score.
Keep that call inside your application code so the result drives normal program logic.
When your categories change, change the label set instead of fine-tuning again, as Glean describes.

playbook.title: Reproduce a paper's claim yourself with its published prompts and a local model
playbook.summary: When a hot paper makes a big claim, run its published prompts against a model on your own machine. Willison did this with a paper's grid-game weights using the llm tool and Qwen 3.8 27B. Treat claims about raw reading and claims about tool use as separate questions.
steps: Find the prompt files in the paper's repository and pass a prompt URL to the llm tool with its fragment option.
Load the local model with a long context window, since the default 8192 failed with errors.
Raise the timeout for the run, because one answer took 46 minutes.
Judge the no-tools question separately from what the model can do once it has code execution.

playbook.title: From May: Cap an agent's blast radius with a sandbox instead of more approval prompts
playbook.who: Anthropic engineers, in How we contain Claude across products
playbook.summary: Anthropic found users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts, so oversight wore thin. It recommends restricting what an agent can reach. Still worth reading because it covers pre-trust configuration risks that newer agent tools repeat.
steps: Run the agent in a sandbox that allows workspace writes and denies network access by default.
Keep credentials out of the sandbox so they cannot be exfiltrated.
Give agents read-only access where possible instead of write access to production.
Defer parsing project-local settings until the user accepts the trust prompt.

audio.script:
Saturday, November 14, 2026. This is The A I Dispatch.

The bottom line. Software agents are starting to spend money, and to be turned away at the door. OpenAI launched a wallet that lets its agents check out on a user's behalf, while United Airlines said it will block outside A I agents from booking flights. Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and a new research claim says some of China's leading open models bear the fingerprints of banned Nvidia chips.

Models first. Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash across its products. According to Ars Technica, Google says it is two and a half times faster than the model it replaces and produces more than five times fewer fabricated claims. Those are Google's own figures. The newsletter Latent Space adds independent measurements from Artificial Analysis, which rated the model strong on hallucination but weaker than two rivals on a terminal coding test. A P I pricing is one dollar fifty per million input tokens and seven dollars fifty per million output tokens. Separately, from November tenth, Latent Space tested a new open weights coding model from a company called Naive A I, which promises very high speed. Its reviewer found the coding quality holds up against DeepSeek, at a slightly higher cost per question.

Research. A report from November eleventh says Google DeepMind used an agent to formally verify key cryptographic guarantees in the Signal protocol in four weeks. The work found no new flaws in the parts it covered, and the researchers say there is a long way to go before this scales. Also today, TechCrunch reports that a researcher named Will DePue analysed the weights of open models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group, and found evidence of training on Blackwell chips, which are banned from export to China. The article notes the chips could have been used in an offshore data center, so a rule may not have been broken. Anthropic published guidance on building strong safety evaluations, and it is also the source of one of today's playbook techniques. And Ars Technica covers a lecture in which Paul Cristiano, a member of the OpenAI Foundation board, said he sees a meaningful risk of an A I takeover. He also said there is no quantitative model behind the number.

Tools and builders. OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets its agents, called dots, complete purchases. It is limited at first to some US Pro subscribers, and users approve each purchase with a fingerprint or face check. Meta's Muse agent can now place phone calls to US businesses for paying subscribers. On the other side, United Airlines said it will restrict unauthorized third party A I agents from booking and managing flights, citing security risks and federal rules. And from November tenth, security firm Claroc reported that shared apps built with Grok Build were exposing private data, including from SpaceXSI itself. The company began removing the links after Ars Technica sent questions.

Policy and industry. From November eleventh, Reuters reported, through Ars Technica, that TSMC's board approved plans to invest up to one billion dollars across Anthropic and OpenAI. Analysts quoted by the Wall Street Journal warned that circular financing makes real demand hard to judge. LangChain raised a three hundred million dollar Series C at a three billion dollar valuation, and says it has seven thousand customers of its LangSmith product.

Now the playbook, four techniques from people who build these tools.

One. From Anthropic, in its post on safety evaluations: score whole conversations, not single replies. Have domain experts write a rubric, pair harmful prompts with harmless ones on the same topic, simulate multi turn chats, and fail the whole conversation if any turn goes wrong.

Two. From Diogo Almeida of Type Safe A I, and Glean's Chinmay Goyal: call a fast system one model inside your code when you need a choice, a score or a probability, and keep large language models for open ended writing.

Three. From Simon Willison: test a paper's claim yourself. Feed the paper's published prompts to a local model with the L L M command line tool, raise the context window above the default, and raise the timeout, because a single run can take close to an hour.

Four, from May, from Anthropic's engineers: limit what an agent can reach with a sandbox. Keep credentials out of it, deny network access by default, and do not read project settings until the user trusts the folder.

Learn one thing. A system one model does not write text. It returns a structured choice, a score or a probability, and it is usually much faster and cheaper than a reasoning model. At the Latent Space code summit this week, speakers argued these models belong inside application code, so that software can make reliable decisions. Glean said it uses one next to large language models and does not need to retrain it when its categories change.

The days ahead. Reports say Anthropic's share pricing is set for next Wednesday, November eighteenth, though Anthropic's own notice gives only the expected range of seventy to seventy eight dollars. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify to House committees by Thanksgiving, November twenty sixth. And Google's Carbon and Argon models are reported to double in price on December first.

That is the brief for Saturday, November fourteenth.
